title: The Mirror: Names, Scores, Seals, and the Honesty of Review

intelligence.essence: Review fails in predictable ways, and each has a named cure: don't promise what isn't proven — write the promise gate into the record with gaps enumerated and the truth state stamped (SN-099); name things what they are (SN-0106); let an independent scorekeeper hold a baseline that scores can fall from (SN-0107); know that a seal proves consistency, not authorship (SN-0111); make verifiers fail closed, never crash (SN-0118), and end every verification by naming what it did not verify (SN-0121); when your numbers diverge from the spec, re-read the spec (SN-0122); lift frozen-baseline values verbatim instead of inventing them (SN-0119); and keep capture controls off output surfaces — the Hub is the screen, not the camera (SN-0124).
intelligence.human_view: This is about keeping every mirror honest. Don't promise what isn't proven — write "not ready yet" where everyone can see it, with the gaps listed. Name things what they are. Let someone other than the builder keep score, and let scores go down. Know exactly what a seal does and doesn't prove. When your work doesn't match the plan, re-read the plan instead of trusting your memory. Copy the approved design exactly instead of improvising. And keep the shop window a window — displays show finished work; they are not where work gets made.
intelligence.child_view: Imagine showing your drawing to the class. You don't say "it's the best drawing ever" before anyone's checked it — you say "not ready yet" if it isn't. You label your crayons with the right colors. The teacher doesn't let you grade your own test, and a grade can go down as well as up — that's how you know it's real. A wax seal on a letter proves nobody opened it; it doesn't prove who wrote it. And if your drawing looks different from the picture you're copying, you look at the picture again — you don't trust your memory.
intelligence.grandma_view: Dear, it's honesty in the small things, which is where honesty lives. Say "not ready" plainly when it isn't. Call things by their right names. Never grade your own work, and let a grade fall when the work falls. Know what a seal guarantees — and what it doesn't. When your memory of the recipe disagrees with the recipe card, believe the card. And a display shelf is for showing what's finished, not for doing the making.
intelligence.ai_view: Gate public claims on named acceptance tests and stamp truth states mechanically (SN-099). Treat misleading names as defects with byte-identical repairs (SN-0106). Refuse self-scoring; defend the baseline; publish falls (SN-0107). State seal scope exactly — consistency, never authorship (SN-0111) — and build verifiers tolerant-reading and fail-closed, never crashing (SN-0118). End every verification with its boundary sentence (SN-0121). On divergence, re-read the spec sections before rebuilding (SN-0122); lift frozen values verbatim and flag inherited warts upward (SN-0119). Keep capture off output surfaces (SN-0124).
intelligence.what_it_means: Nine notes are the team's reflective surface: the disciplines that keep names, scores, seals, reports, and claims telling the truth about the work. A cold reader holding only this essence can still review the way these notes demand — and can spot each named way review goes dishonest.
whats_inside: Claims stop at the promise gate: gaps enumerated, truth state stamped, gate test named — in the product record, before any public promise (SN-099); fork isolation law precedes the first fork (SN-099).
Names must say what the thing is; a lying name is repaired by byte-identical rename with zero stragglers (SN-0106).
Scorekeeping is independent, baselines are law, and scores must be able to fall (SN-0107).
Seal = consistency, not authorship (SN-0111); verifiers fail closed and never crash on admissible input (SN-0118); every verification names its unverified remainder (SN-0121).
Divergence from the spec is resolved by re-reading the spec, not by trusting memory (SN-0122); frozen-baseline values are lifted verbatim (SN-0119).
Output surfaces never grow input controls (SN-0124).
